Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenThe Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said he welcomed the report’s call for a comprehensive security framework. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAZack PolanskiZack Polanski backs report endorsing Nato membership and maintaining nuclear weaponsPosition contrasts with Green party’s policies before 2024 election, as polls show just 17% of voters trust them on defence

Prefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski has given his backing to a paper that endorses Britain’s membership of Nato and the maintenance of the country’s nuclear weapons.

The Green party leader has welcomed a report from the Verdant thinktank that says the UK should remain in the military alliance and calls for the country to cooperate more closely with France on the maintenance of its nuclear weapons.

Party sources stress that its defence policies remain unchanged since 2024, when it went into the last election calling for the UK to sign the UN treaty on the prohibition of nuclear weapons and immediately begin dismantling its Trident submarines.

However, they added that Polanski’s endorsement of the report was part of a debate taking place within the party on how to reassure a broader group of voters on national security issues.

Polanski said: “At its core, national security is about food on the table, warm homes and safe communities. That makes it a progressive issue – and I welcome Verdant’s call for a comprehensive security framework that brings people from across the UK into keeping our country safe.”

Sacha Deshmukh, the author of the report, said: “Historically some progressives have shied away from recognising security threats. But the right has not been willing to accept the flaws in their policy solutions, so they are not always as strong as they should be – both sides need to change that.”

National security has often been seen as one of the Green party’s weak points with a YouGov poll last year showing just 17% of voters trusted the Greens on defence – the lowest of 18 different issues.

Concerns over the Greens’ positions on defence have driven some members to call for it to end its opposition to drones and anti-ballistic missiles, something that caused an internal rift ahead of its conference this year.

The Verdant report is likely to trigger another round of debate within the party, given that the thinktank, while independent, retains close links to the Greens.

The report calls for the government to rethink its national security strategy to focus more on value for money, such as by buying more weapons off the shelf rather than designing high-end bespoke systems for use by the British military.

It also calls for more investment in climate adaptation – something some in the green movement view sceptically as taking attention away from efforts to stop the climate deteriorating in the first place.

In two policy areas, however, Deshmukh calls for government policy to remain largely the same, despite previous calls from the Green party and Polanski personally for more radical change.

On Nato, he calls for the UK to remain a member but push for reform of its structures alongside allies within the alliance.

Such a position mirrors the official Green party policy, but contradicts what Polanski has previously said is his personal view.

He told the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast earlier this year: “Donald Trump has so much domination within Nato that I don’t believe it’s possible to reform Nato from within.”

And on the nuclear deterrent, Deshmukh argues the UK could not, and potentially should not, cancel the contract for the next generation of nuclear submarines, known as Dreadnought.

However, he adds that the country should seek to cooperate more closely with France on the missiles that will equip it, even though it is being developed to carry the US Trident missiles, which the UK currently uses.

Any form of commitment to the nuclear deterrent would be a sharp contrast to the promise the Greens made before the last election, when it said elected members would push for the UK to begin dismantling its nuclear weapons immediately.
